sections.title: Introduction
sections.content: This report covers your Holloway Stocks & Shares ISAs (Robert and Jean), the joint General Investment Account (GIA), and a proposed new joint investment account. We are authorised and regulated by the Financial Conduct Authority.

sections.title: Background & Objectives
sections.content:
Your objectives remain the same as at your last review: you are seeking long-term growth and do not require income from your portfolio for the foreseeable future. You both remain comfortable with a moderate level of investment risk (risk score 4). Jean has received an inheritance following the recent death of her mother, and you wish to invest these funds alongside your existing holdings.

sections.title: Recommendations
sections.content:
We recommend disinvesting the full balance of your joint GIA and combining these proceeds with the inheritance received by Jean (around £120,000), to fund top-ups for both Robert’s and Jean’s ISAs for the new tax year. The balance remaining after the ISA contributions should then be invested into a new jointly-held investment account. This approach seeks to make use of available tax-advantaged wrappers for long-term growth.

The agreed initial charge for this advice and implementation is 0.5% of the invested amount. Any applicable ongoing platform and advice charges will be set out in the next section; please see Fees & Charges below.

Please note that the proposed new joint account is not yet opened; the precise account details and final investment amounts should be agreed and confirmed prior to proceeding.

sections.title: Tax Implications
sections.content: Selling down the joint GIA may give rise to a capital gains tax liability, which would be assessed against each client’s annual exempt amount for capital gains. The precise amount of any gain and the resulting tax position must be reviewed and confirmed prior to disinvestment.

sections.title: Conclusion
sections.content:
The value of investments can fall as well as rise and you may get back less than you invest. Past performance is not a guide to future returns.
